en.title: Possessives: my, your, his
en.summary: Possessive words such as my, your and his show who owns or has something.

paragraphs: Possessives show who owns something or to whom it belongs. They also show relationships and parts of the body. The English possessives that stand before a noun are my, your, his, her, its, our and their. They belong to a group called determiners.

A possessive agrees with the owner, not with the thing owned. We say his mother for a man's mother and her mother for a woman's mother. Do not use an article with a possessive. For a noun owner, add 's to the name or noun: Tom's car, the children's toys.
Its is the possessive: The dog wagged its tail. It's is the short form of it is or it has: It's late. The possessive its has no apostrophe, just like his and hers.
English uses a possessive for parts of the body and clothes, where some languages use an article. We say She broke her arm and He put on his coat.

items: Wrong: **The dog wagged it's tail.** Right: **The dog wagged its tail.**
Wrong: **Tom took her bag.** (his own bag) Right: **Tom took his bag.**

ro.title: Posesivele: meu, tău, său
ro.summary: Adjectivele posesive arată cui aparține un lucru și stau de obicei după un substantiv cu articol hotărât.

paragraphs: Posesivele arată cui aparține un obiect sau o persoană. În limba română folosim cuvinte precum „meu”, „tău” sau „său”. Substantivul din fața posesivului primește de obicei articol hotărât.
Posesivul se acordă în gen și număr cu obiectul posedat, nu cu posesorul. Substantivul din fața lui are aproape mereu articol hotărât la sfârșit.
